faq.question: Explain the DBWhisper RAG / agent architecture.
faq.answer: DBWhisper is a LangGraph agent that turns plain English into safe, read-only SQL. When a database is enrolled, its schema is introspected, AI-documented into structured sections (summary, columns, relationships, stats), and embedded into pgvector. At query time the agent runs a tightly-scoped tool loop: semantic-search the schema to find candidate tables, fetch only the sections it needs (keeping the prompt small), look for a human-approved verified question-to-SQL example to adapt, generate dialect-correct SQL, and then pass it through a fail-closed read-only validator before executing. It's RAG over a schema rather than stuffing the whole schema into the prompt, which keeps each prompt to the few tables a question needs. Retrieval has not been benchmarked at scale yet: the largest schema enrolled in the repository has 16 tables. Conversation memory is persisted to Postgres via a LangGraph checkpoint so follow-ups have context.

faq.question: How does DBWhisper stop the LLM from running dangerous SQL?
faq.answer: It validates generated SQL before execution, and the model is never trusted to. Since DBWhisper v2 (24 August 2026), every statement passes a SQLGlot AST policy engine (app/sqlpolicy, sql_policy@2.0.0), with the original keyword heuristics kept as an independent second layer; the stricter result wins, and app/core/sql_validator.py is now a thin wrapper over it. The engine parses the query in its target dialect and admits a single read-only SELECT or WITH; it rejects DML, DDL, GRANT/REVOKE, EXEC, multiple statements, SELECT INTO, system-catalog access (information_schema, pg_catalog, sys.*), a list of blocked functions, and tables outside the database's enrolled schema. It is fail-closed: when a database is named and its enrolled schema cannot be loaded, the query is refused. Its decisions are regression-tested against an adversarial corpus committed in the repository (the deterministic policy test on /evals). It is a structural filter, not a proof: its guarantee is bounded by how faithfully SQLGlot parses each dialect. Further controls: a least-privilege login, read-only database sessions on PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQLite (SQL Server has no session-level read-only mode), query timeouts and row caps, and log sanitization that masks passwords and API keys. These are specific enforcement layers; they do not establish a universal guarantee against data exposure or service failure.

faq.question: How does he make sure the metrics his products show are real, not faked?
faq.answer: It's the single rule running through everything he builds: every number a user sees is genuinely computed. TradePulse is the clearest example — its backtester is structurally look-ahead-free (decisions read only closed bars; orders fill on the next bar's open), models commission and slippage on every fill by default, always shows drawdown, and states its risk-free-rate-of-zero assumption wherever Sharpe appears. Its correctness test suite even perturbs future bars and proves past equity is unchanged. DBWhisper publishes its policy result as a deterministic test, not as model accuracy, and when its own claim audit found that two earlier figures could not be reproduced, they were retired in public with the reason. Both projects also publish what they deliberately do NOT claim.
faq.source: TradePulse — backtesting engine + tests; DBWhisper — claim audit + /evals; profile ethos

faq.question: Why the free-tier / $0 infrastructure stack?
faq.answer: Partly because he's a solo builder self-funding these products, but mostly because the constraint forces discipline. Running on Hugging Face Spaces, Vercel, and Neon with $0 infra means no waste is possible: lean Docker images, small prompts via section-scoped retrieval, bounded agent loops, quota checks before spending a shared API key, and multi-provider fallback chains that keep a free tier alive when one provider is exhausted. The free-tier limits shaped the engineering from the start rather than being optimized in later — and it proves he can ship a full multi-user SaaS shape without hiding behind an expensive managed stack.
faq.source: profile stats · about narrative · DBWhisper deployment

faq.answer: It's his current full-time work at Sevina Technologies (2024–present), where his flagship products include CareLTC, NFC room rounds for long-term care, which he leads; the CareLTC case study has the details. faq.question: Can he really do end-to-end, or just the AI/model layer?
faq.answer: End-to-end, and the work is the proof. Bench Discovery spans a web platform on AWS and a Windows desktop app that he designed, built and maintains; CareLTC spans iOS and Android apps, an API with a scheduler and an admin portal, and he leads it and did the main engineering work. Across the public projects he owns the whole loop too: LLM agents and RAG retrieval strategies; FastAPI backends with async, auth, and tenancy; Next.js frontends; Postgres/pgvector/Redis data layers; and the deployment itself — Docker images, HTTPS, CI pipelines, and security hardening. His earlier role at Linescripts (2022–2024) was full-stack web delivery (Django/DRF, REST APIs, frontends), so the end-to-end habit predates the AI work.
faq.source: Bench Discovery · CareLTC · public projects · Sevina + Linescripts roles · skills

faq.question: What's his experience with LLM agents and multi-provider routing?
faq.answer: Substantial and hands-on. DBWhisper is a full LangGraph/LangChain agent with a custom toolset and a six-provider fallback chain (OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Groq, Anthropic, Gemini), with Gemini configured as the final fallback. TradePulse's copilot receives computed data and is prompted to use only the supplied figures. At Sevina he built GenAI assistants with multi-provider routing across OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini. Multi-provider routing is a recurring pattern in his work — for resilience and to avoid single-vendor lock-in.
faq.source: DBWhisper agent · TradePulse copilot · Sevina role

faq.question: How does he keep AI copilots from hallucinating numbers?
faq.answer: By grounding them and letting them refuse. TradePulse's copilot generates a validated strategy spec (via a validate-and-repair loop) and never auto-executes it; its narration prompt says to use ONLY the numbers present in the provided data — never invent, estimate, or extrapolate — and to close with a fixed not-financial-advice line. It degrades to a deterministic data summary when no API key is present, and DBWhisper's validator, not the model, decides whether generated SQL may run. The design principle: a financial or predictive AI should refuse before it guesses.

faq.question: Why hire him — what's the strongest evidence of his engineering judgment (senior-level thinking)?
faq.answer: The trade-offs he makes deliberately, and the limits he documents. In Bench Discovery, “documents stay on this computer” is proved by tests over the compiled binaries rather than promised; every redacted copy is checked the way an attacker would check it, and a failed check places no file; and the evidence score ships uncalibrated, with that said plainly. In CareLTC, the server decides whether a tap completes a round, rounds nobody could do are excused rather than deleted, and a resident sync that would discharge too many residents at once changes nothing. In the public projects, DBWhisper fails closed when generated SQL violates its validator rules, and TradePulse fills orders on the next bar with a canary test for look-ahead leakage. The case studies explain each trade-off and the evidence behind it.
faq.source: Bench Discovery · CareLTC · DBWhisper validator · TradePulse spec + tests

faq.question: Has he found and fixed real production bugs?
faq.answer: Yes — the kind that only show up on real devices. In CareLTC, every NFC scan on iPhones failed with “Duplicated registration”: iOS marks the app inactive while the system NFC sheet is open, and the scan screen treated that as leaving the app, tearing down the very session that had opened the sheet. He traced it and changed the screen to stop scanning only when the app really moves to the background, with a bounded retry for that one error. It is a good illustration of why he tests on the devices and data people actually use rather than trusting that a simulator is representative.
faq.source: CareLTC — case study (what broke, and what changed)

faq.question: How does he approach security and production hardening?
faq.answer: As a default, not an afterthought. Recurring across the products: Argon2id password hashing and DB-backed revocable sessions with HttpOnly SameSite cookies; strict per-user tenancy; a fail-closed read-only SQL validator with read-only DB users and log sanitization; rate limiting; strict Content-Security-Policy, HSTS, and other security headers; upload size/MIME limits; DSN-gated Sentry; and CI gates that run linting, tests and dependency audits. Server-side-only API keys and no-PII logging are standard.
faq.source: DBWhisper SECURITY.md · this site's security headers and CI

faq.question: How does TradePulse avoid look-ahead bias?
faq.answer: By construction rather than by convention. The engine decides on a closed bar and fills market orders on the next bar's open, so a strategy can never act on a price it only knew after the bar closed. Strategies are written in a declarative, non-Turing-complete spec whose operands can only read indicators and price fields on closed bars, so look-ahead cannot even be expressed. Indicators warm up with honest null gaps instead of producing values from bar 0. A canary test perturbs every future bar 3× and checks that equity up to the cut bar is byte-identical, so a leak fails the build. The cost is a bar of latency between signal and fill, accepted because the alternative is measuring a strategy you can't actually trade.

faq.question: Does this assistant store my question? What happens to what I type?
faq.answer: Your question is used to write one answer, and this site doesn't store it: there is no transcript, and the one log line kept per answer records how it was answered, its timings and token counts — never the question, the answer or your address. To write a live answer, the question and the recent conversation are sent to Google's Gemini API. The site uses Gemini's free tier, on which Google may use what is sent to improve its products and people at Google may review it, so don't type anything confidential. In the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the UK, where Google's terms don't allow the free tier, answers come from site search alone and nothing is sent to Gemini. The conversation lives only in the open tab and is gone when it closes or reloads.

faq.question: How does this assistant work, and where do its answers come from?
faq.answer: It searches this site's own pages — the case studies, writing, evaluations, the résumé, and the hiring and contact pages — and answers only from the passages it finds, linking the pages they come from. When no page covers a question, it says so instead of guessing. When live answers are available, Google's Gemini model writes the answer from those passages; otherwise it shows the best passage as written. Answers can be imperfect, so check the page each one cites.
